title: Low-depth simulation of non-Markovianity under quantum hardware noise
abstract: Simulating open quantum systems on digital quantum computers typically relies on the use of auxiliary qubits, resulting in overheads of noisy multi-qubit gates, that severely limit execution on near-term hardware. In this work, we explore the simulation of non-Markovian dynamics as well as memory channels leveraging the method of trajectory mixing, valid for mixed unitary channels. This allows to drastically reduce circuit depth, trading entangling gates for a statistical mixture of independent, pure state trajectories. Using a realistic noise model calibrated to modern quantum processors, we show the benefits of this approach, yielding higher state fidelity and better preservation of quantum correlations. This shows the possibility of simulating long-time non-Markovian evolutions with low noise and limited resources.
summary: This paper introduces trajectory mixing as an efficient alternative to standard auxiliary qubit methods for simulating open quantum systems. By statistically averaging over independent pure state trajectories, it drastically reduces circuit depth and gate overheads when modeling non-Markovian dynamics under realistic quantum noise models. This makes long-time simulation of complex quantum processes more feasible on near-term hardware.
main_problem: The primary challenge is efficiently simulating non-Markovian dynamics of open quantum systems on near-term digital quantum computers while minimizing noise overheads from auxiliary qubits.
main_result: The method of trajectory mixing drastically reduces circuit depth compared to standard Stinespring dilation, yielding higher state fidelity for simulating complex, long-time non-Markovian evolutions.
method: The authors employ trajectory mixing, which simulates the open channel as a statistical mixture of independent, pure state trajectories, avoiding the need for auxiliary qubits and associated high-overhead entangling gates.
model_or_system: The work models open quantum systems undergoing non-Markovian dynamics or memory channels. Specific examples include dephasing and amplitude damping processes driven by stochastic Hamiltonians (like Random Telegraph Noise).
key_observables: State fidelity with respect to noiseless evolution, concurrence (for entanglement preservation), and the BLP measure (to confirm non-Markovianity).
important_parameters: Noise model parameters include single-qubit relaxation ($T_1$), phase loss ($T_2$), and CNOT depolarization rates. The method is restricted to mixed unitary channels.
main_assumptions: The trajectory mixing approach assumes the channel is a statistical mix of unitaries with state-independent jump probabilities; furthermore, stochastic sampling (Monte Carlo) is used to circumvent the exponential scaling of total trajectories.
figures_summary: Figures compare dynamics and fidelity for dephasing/memory channels using mixed trajectories versus auxiliary qubits. Later figures show high fidelity maintenance over time steps when simulating non-Markovian evolution via a stochastic Hamiltonian.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the limitations of standard simulation techniques (Stinespring dilation). It then proposes and demonstrates trajectory mixing for simple dephasing, extends this to memory channels using concurrence analysis, and finally applies it successfully to complex non-Markovian dynamics driven by a stochastic Hamiltonian.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial algorithmic improvement for quantum simulation, offering a resource-efficient pathway to model realistic open system dynamics that are otherwise computationally prohibitive due to noise overheads on current hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Simple dephasing. (a) Dynamics in the bloch sphere for a qubit under pure dephasing, simulated using mixed trajectories (green stars), and using auxiliary qubits (orange diamonds) as well as the noisless dynamics (gray square). Notice how the mixed trajectory dynamics and the noiseless dynamics are almost overlapping with one another, while the auxiliary qubits dynamics is drifting more towards the centre of the sphere. This is further shown in (b), where we show that the dynamics simulated via mixed trajectories (green stars) retains much higher values of state fidelity with the noiseless dynamics, as opposed to the dynamics simulated via auxiliary qubits (orange diamonds).

FIG. 2. Non-Markovian amplitude damping. (a) Dynamics in the bloch sphere for a qubit undergoing non-Markovian amplitude damping, simulated using mixed trajectories (green stars), and using auxiliary qubits (orange diamonds) as well as the noisless dynamics (gray square). Here, both the mixed trajectory and the auxiliary qubits dynamics are drifting more towards the centre of the sphere, compared to the noiseless dynamics. In (b) we compare the fidelity, with respect to the noiseless dynamics, of the mixed trajectories and the auxiliary qubits methods. We consider both the system alone (green stars and orange diamonds) and the system and memory together (dark green stars and dark orange...

FIG. 3. Non-Markovian dephasing. Fidelity values with respect to the noiseless dynamics. Also in this case the mixed trajectories method offers better values of fidelity in general, but the auxiliary qubits method can occasionally perform better while looking at the system only.

FIG. 4. Entanglement under memory channels. We show the concurrence of two qubits initially prepared in a bell state, under the repeated action of a memory channel. When the memory channel is simulated via mixed trajectories entanglement is highly preserved, while it decays considerably when the memory channel is simulated via auxiliary qubits.

FIG. 5. Long time evolutions. Fidelity with respect to the noiseless dynamics for the simple dephasing (a) and concurrence under repeated action of a memory channel (b), simulated for 25 time steps. Even though we only simulate a fraction of all the possible trajectories, the mixed trajectories method performs significantly better than the auxiliary qubits one.
